title: What happens to mathematics when AI becomes an oracle?
gist: Interview with Steven Strogatz on his book Big Math (with Alex Townsend), arguing computers have moved from servant to scout to oracle: AI now produces right-seeming results it cannot explain. He suggests mathematics may have to adopt the empirical validation methods of medicine, at real epistemic and cultural cost, while staying hopeful about AI as teacher and discovery engine.

insights.claim: Steven Strogatz frames the history of computing in mathematics as three stages: computer as servant (doing calculations we specify), scout (exploring unknown territory as in the 1950s Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou experiment), and now oracle (producing results we cannot understand and it cannot explain).
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Useful lens for where AI-for-science value accrues: answers without explanations.
insights.locator: Strogatz: So from servant to scout

insights.claim: The Fermi-Pasta-Ulam numerical experiment unexpectedly showed 98 percent of the energy returning to the original vibration mode instead of decaying to entropy, birthing soliton theory and showing human intuition breaks down in nonlinear systems.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Historical precedent that computational exploration can create entire new fields.
insights.locator: So they ran it in the computer

insights.claim: AlphaFold lets scientists solve a thousand times more protein structures than before without yielding new physics or chemistry, exemplifying AI-as-oracle pattern recognition without explanation.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: AI value in science may come from throughput, not insight — relevant to drug discovery economics.

insights.claim: Strogatz expects the opacity of AI results to get worse, and believes some AI-produced findings will remain truly opaque to humans even with AI's help because of human speed, intelligence and memory limits.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Validation and verification tooling becomes a structural need as AI output outpaces human comprehension.
insights.quote: So that’s where we are, and it’s going to get worse.

insights.claim: If AI becomes an oracle, mathematics may need to shift toward the methods of medicine and engineering — checking empirically how often the oracle is right, like FDA trials that approve drugs without known mechanisms of action.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Suggests a market for empirical AI benchmarking and verification in high-stakes science.
insights.quote: If the AI is an oracle, you can still check it by seeing how often it is right.
insights.locator: Then I think math starts to be more like science

insights.claim: Moving mathematics from proof-based certainty to empirical validation would be an epistemic loss, since pure math is the only discipline with absolute proof (Euclid's proofs from 300 BC remain valid).
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Resistance from pure mathematicians may slow acceptance of AI-generated results without formal proofs.

insights.claim: Stephen Wolfram's computational irreducibility thesis holds that most of nature has no compressed, insightful description and can only be simulated; Strogatz agrees many simulations are irreducible but doubts nature is.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Frames whether AI simulation can replace theory-driven science.

insights.claim: Strogatz defines 'big math' as math that is big relative to human cognitive capacity, such as the lunar module computer steering with only 20-30 variables, rather than math with big numbers.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Reframes AI/computing advantage around problems that exceed human working memory.

insights.claim: Linear and sparse problems scale to immense size and remain tractable, while big nonlinear problems lie in 'terra incognita' for rigorous theorems and can only be handled computationally.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Explains why large-scale computation (e.g., LLMs with trillions of parameters) outruns theoretical understanding.
insights.locator: Big Math is not simply big

insights.claim: Moon Duchin's ensemble method generates thousands of random legally-compliant redistricting maps as a baseline, allowing a gerrymandered map to be identified as an extreme statistical outlier.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Computational ensembles are a practical tool in redistricting litigation.
insights.locator: Nevertheless, Moon Duchin and her colleagues

insights.claim: Strogatz says the US Supreme Court is very resistant to mathematical evidence and, after the book went to press, ruled that partisan gerrymandering does not violate the Voting Rights Act.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Legal acceptance of quantitative evidence remains limited, constraining its policy impact.

insights.claim: OpenAI released 722 AI-generated math papers in October 2026, dubbed the 'mathocalypse', alarming many mathematicians.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: AI labs are producing mathematical research at volume, a signal of accelerating AI-for-science capability.
insights.locator: Ars: The rapid rise of AI in mathematics

insights.claim: Strogatz expects AI to make the greatest mathematical discoveries going forward, with humans left to make smaller discoveries while still enjoying math recreationally.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The frontier of discovery is shifting to AI systems and the labs that run them.
insights.locator: And why do we have to feel sad?

insights.claim: Young aspiring mathematicians face grief as some in the tech community proclaim the subject 'over', while creative-writing faculty report similar distress over AI-generated student work.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: AI disruption of knowledge professions creates talent-pipeline and cultural backlash risks.

insights.claim: Current AIs are poor at asking good research questions, but Strogatz believes they could be trained to do so, as PhD students are.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Question-generation is a remaining human edge and a likely next target for AI research agents.
insights.quote: So far the AIs are not good at asking questions.
insights.locator: Strogatz: So far the AIs are not good

insights.claim: Strogatz sees AI as potentially an effective math teacher and expects astonishing practical benefits in energy, climate, medicine and physics, calling the moment both joyful and confusing.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Balanced view: AI-for-science upside in energy, climate and medicine is large even amid displacement.
insights.locator: There is a feeling of loss
